prompt_summary: Bubblegum Bay sandy cove with left-middle plaza path, open beach, turquoise water, rope-railed dock, blank welcome sign, palms, picnic umbrella and blanket, shells, driftwood, beach toys, and corner rocks. No people, animals, buildings, or lettering.

scale_reference.canvas: 1750x1100 logical units at 2 source px per unit
scale_reference.palm: about 360 logical units / 720 source px, 2.57 Fae heights
scale_reference.picnicBlanket: about 210 logical units / 420 source px, 1.5 Fae lengths
scale_reference.beachBall: about 48 logical units / 96 source px, approximately Fae head width

post_processing: The raw 2528x1696 generation (art/source/areas/bay/bay-raw.png) is resized and cropped once: magick bay-raw.png -filter Lanczos -resize 3500x -gravity center -crop 3500x2200+0+0 +repage (a uniform 1.384x upscale, as the school's 1.4x; 74 source px trimmed from the top and bottom).
Split into two opaque 1750x2200 WebP tiles at quality 88: -crop 1750x2200+0+0 and +1750+0.
Paper margin colour #fcfbf6 recorded in ground.json.
geometry: Authored by hand against the painting, like the other areas, and checked against the paint itself: tools/art/paint-map.ts reads the tiles into a 5-unit map (water, sand, painted things, edges; tests/unit/fixtures/bay-paint.json). tests/unit/bay-paint.test.ts requires no open water inside the floor, at most 2% of open sand off it or under blockers, every blocker on something painted, and the dock walkable rail to rail. tests/unit/bay-depth.test.ts requires the near (south) rail drawn over Fae on the dock and never over her on the beach (25-unit rail slivers, each with the baseline of its east end, since one baseline can't fit a diagonal rail), the far rail never over her, the umbrella, sign, and palm trunks over her behind them, and every occluder on its object. The floor excludes the rock piles along the top (x 200-550) and at the right; blockers stand on the trunk feet, sign posts, picnic, umbrella shade, bucket, beach balls, logs, and the dock's rail where the beach meets it.
